segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For this reason, since we have this ministry as people who were shown mercy, we do not lose heart.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Rather, we have renounced the shameful, hidden things; we do not walk in cunning or tamper with the word of God, but by the open display of the truth we commend ourselves to every person’s conscience in the sight of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And even if our good news is veiled, it is veiled among those who are perishing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: among whom the god of this age has blinded the minds of the unbelievers, so that they do not see the light of the good news of the glory of Christ, who is the image of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we do not proclaim ourselves, but Christ Jesus as Lord, and ourselves as your slaves for Jesus’s sake.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is the God who said,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “Out of darkness light will shine,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who has shone in our hearts to give the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we have this treasure in clay jars, so that the surpassing greatness of the power may be God’s and not from us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We are afflicted in every way but not crushed, at a loss but not at a total loss,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: persecuted but not abandoned, struck down but not perishing,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: always carrying around in the body the dying of Jesus, so that the life of Jesus may also be displayed in our body.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we who live are constantly being handed over to death for Jesus’s sake, so that the life of Jesus may also be displayed in our mortal flesh.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, death is at work in us, but life in you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But since we have the same spirit of faith, in keeping with what is written,

segments.speaker: scripture
segments.text: “I believed, therefore I spoke,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: we also believe, and therefore we also speak,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: knowing that the one who raised Jesus will raise us also with Jesus and will present us together with you.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For all of this is for your sake, so that grace, increasing through more and more people, may make thanksgiving overflow to the glory of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore we do not lose heart. Even if our outer self is wasting away, our inner self is being renewed day by day.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the momentary lightness of our affliction is producing for us, beyond all measure, an eternal weight of glory,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: as we fix our eyes not on the things that are seen but on the things that are not seen. For the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal.

notes.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for the announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. 'Gospel' has become a religious term or a book title, so the plainer rendering is used. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The Greek word means an age or era, not the physical world. Paul shares the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Nearly all interpreters take the phrase to refer to Satan, as the power that holds sway in the present age. A few ancient interpreters took it to mean God himself.

notes.traditional: lest the light ... should shine unto them
notes.note: The verb can mean either 'see clearly' or 'shine'. On the second reading the clause means 'so that the light of the good news does not shine on them', as in older English versions. Most modern translations take it as 'see', which fits the image of blinded minds.

The word denotes a slave, a person owned by another, not a hired servant. Traditional versions soften it to 'servants'. Paul sets the word deliberately against 'Lord': Jesus is the master, and his envoys are at the Corinthians' disposal on his account.

This is not an exact quotation of any one passage. It recalls God's command at creation, 'Let there be light' (Genesis 1:3), and may also echo Isaiah 9:2, where light shines on those living in darkness. Paul presents the coming of the good news as a new act of creation.

notes.traditional: in the face of Jesus Christ
notes.note: Many manuscripts read 'Jesus Christ' here, and some 'Christ Jesus'. The edition translated reads simply 'Christ'. The meaning is not affected.

Fired-clay pottery was the cheap, everyday container of the ancient world, easily broken and thrown away when damaged. The contrast is between the worth of the contents and the fragility of the container. The container is the messengers themselves in their bodily weakness.

notes.phrase: at a loss but not at a total loss
notes.note: The Greek plays on two forms of the same verb, the second strengthened by a prefix. The traditional rendering gives the sense but uses two unrelated words. The rendering here keeps the wordplay.

The phrase may mean a disposition of faith, the same attitude as the psalmist's. It may instead refer to the Holy Spirit as the one who produces faith, in which case 'Spirit' would be capitalised. Interpreters are divided; the lower-case rendering follows most translations.

The quotation is from Psalm 116:10, in the wording of the ancient Greek translation, where it is numbered Psalm 115:1. The Hebrew text of that line is difficult and is usually translated differently. The psalm is a thanksgiving by someone rescued from death, which suits Paul's argument here.

notes.phrase: increasing through more and more people
notes.note: The Greek word order allows 'through more and more people' to go with either verb. Either grace increases as it reaches more people, or grace, having increased, makes thanksgiving overflow through the many who give thanks. The Greek also plays on 'grace' and 'thanksgiving', and on 'increase' and 'more', which are related words.

Paul sets 'momentary' against 'eternal' and 'lightness' against 'weight'. Many scholars think the image of glory as heavy reflects Hebrew, in which the word for 'glory' comes from a root meaning 'to be heavy'. This is plausible for a bilingual writer but cannot be proved.

candidates.reason: Translations vary between 'servant', 'slave' and 'bondservant' across the New Testament, and the choice affects how readers hear Paul's self-descriptions and the parables.
It is rendered 'world', 'age' or 'forever' in different contexts, and the two-ages framework is lost if 'this age' and 'this world' alternate without a rule.
Its range in Paul (body, human frailty, sinful nature) leads translators to very different English, and a single policy is needed on when to keep 'flesh'.
'Ministry', 'service' and 'mission' are all used for this word and its cognates, and 'ministry' now carries clerical overtones the Greek lacked.
It is rendered 'tribulation', 'affliction', 'trouble', 'distress' and 'suffering' across books, which obscures a recurring theme. It should be decided together with the verb θλίβω.

patch.reason: euangelion promoted to active after full-run drift (good news 37 / gospel 35)
